blocks.x: MATH 157 · Algebra 9

The gateway topic to calculus: how a function maps one set to another, how to pin down its domain, and what it means for f(x) to approach a value — the idea on which all of differential and integral calculus is built.
2domain-restricting rules — zero denominators and negative even-indexed radicals 8Limit Theorems for sums, products, quotients and powers of limits 3conditions for continuity of f at a point x = a
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Work with functions — evaluate f(x) at given values, find the domain and range, and recognise when a function is undefined.
2Evaluate limits directly using the eight Limit Theorems, and understand left-hand and right-hand limits and when a two-sided limit exists.
3Evaluate limits at infinity and limits of the form lim 1/xⁿ, and compute the classic trigonometric limit lim sin x / x = 1 and its relatives.
4Test continuity of a function at a point and on an interval, using the three-condition definition and the standard continuity rules.

blocks.x: Key definitions
Function A rule that assigns to each element of a set X one and only one element in a set Y. X is the domain, Y is the co-domain. Written f : X ⟶ Y. For each x ∈ X, f(x) ∈ Y is the image of x.
Range The set of all images actually produced by f. The range is a subset of the co-domain — it may or may not equal the whole co-domain.

Limit of a function
lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means as x gets arbitrarily close to a (without necessarily equalling a), f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L.
Existence of a two-sided limit lim_{x→a} f(x) = L if and only if lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) = lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) = L — the left-hand and right-hand limits must agree.
Continuity at a point f is continuous at x = a if (1) f(a) is defined, (2) lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, and (3) f(a) = lim_{x→a} f(x).
Functions→ Evaluating Limits→ Limits & Infinity→ Continuity
Mapping one set to another
A function assigns to every element of a set X one and only one element of a set Y. Evaluating a function and finding its largest possible domain are the two core skills here.

f : X ⟶ Y X is the domain of the function, Y is the co-domain. Some elements of Y may not be an image of any element of X. If every element of Y is an image of some element of X, then Y is called the range of the function. A function can also be defined as a set of ordered pairs: {(a,b) : a ∈ A and b ∈ B}.
Evaluating a function
Let f : A ⟶ B be defined by f(x) = 2x + 3. Evaluate f(0), f(1), f(-3) and f(a).

items: 1Substitute x = 0 into the rule.f(0) = 2(0) + 3 = 3
2Substitute x = 1.f(1) = 2(1) + 3 = 5
4Substitute the general symbol x = a — the rule is applied exactly the same way.f(a) = 2a + 3

blocks.x: Range of a rational function
f : x ⟶ (3x-1)/(x-3) is defined on {-2,-1,0,1,2}. Find the range of f, and state which value of x makes f undefined.

items: 1Substitute each domain value in turn: x = -2.f(-2) = (3(-2)-1)/(-2-3) = -7/-5 = 7/5

blocks.x: Range = {7/5, 1, 1/3, -1, -5}. The function is undefined at x = 3 (denominator zero) — not in the given domain, so no issue here.
Determining the domain of a function

Two rules for excluding x-values To find the largest possible domain, exclude: (1) values of x that make the denominator of a rational function zero, and (2) values of x that produce a negative sign under an even-indexed radical (square root, fourth root, etc.).
State the largest possible domain of f(x) = (1-2x)/√(2x-1).

items: 1The radical is even-indexed (square root), so its contents must be strictly positive (it also sits in the denominator, so it cannot be zero either).2x - 1 > 0
2Solve the inequality for x.2x > 1 → x > ½

blocks.x: Domain: x > ½, i.e. x ∈ (½, ∞)
State the largest possible domain of g(x) = √(1 - x²).

items: 1The expression under the even-indexed radical must be ≥ 0 (it is not in a denominator here, so equality is allowed).1 - x² ≥ 0
2Rearrange to isolate x².x² ≤ 1
3Take square roots — this gives a double-sided inequality.-1 ≤ x ≤ 1

blocks.x: Domain: [-1, 1]
State the largest possible domain of f(x) = (√(x-2)) / (x²-4).

items: 1Radical condition: the numerator's contents must be ≥ 0.x - 2 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 2
2Denominator condition: x² - 4 ≠ 0, so factor and exclude the roots.(x-2)(x+2) ≠ 0 → x ≠ 2, x ≠ -2
3Combine both conditions: x ≥ 2 already excludes x = -2, but x = 2 must also be removed.x ≥ 2 and x ≠ 2 → x > 2

blocks.x: Domain: x > 2, i.e. x ∈ (2, ∞)

blocks.x: State the largest possible domain of:
Tip: a polynomial like f(x) = 1 - 2x has no restrictions — its domain is all of ℝ.
The foundation of calculus
Differential and integral calculus both depend on the limit concept: the behaviour of f(x) as x approaches — but does not necessarily reach — a value a.

The meaning of x ⟶ a For a given function f, x ⟶ a describes the behaviour of f(x) for values of x around a. Consider f(x) = 2x+3 near x = 2: as x approaches 2 from either side, f(x) approaches 7. We write lim_{x→2} (2x+3) = 7.
The eight Limit Theorems

c: lim{f(x)/g(x)} = lim f(x) / lim g(x), provided lim g(x) ≠ 0

blocks.x: Direct substitution
Evaluate lim_{x→4} (2x + 3).

items: 1The function is a polynomial, so it has no restrictions — substitute x = 4 directly (Theorems 2, 3, 4).2(4) + 3
2Simplify.= 8 + 3 = 11

blocks.x: Answer: lim_{x→4} (2x+3) = 11
Indeterminate form 0/0 — factor and cancel
Evaluate lim_{x→1} (x²-1)/(x-1).

items: 1Direct substitution gives 0/0 — an indeterminate form, so factor the numerator first.x² - 1 = (x-1)(x+1)
2Cancel the common factor (x-1), valid since x ≠ 1 as x only approaches 1.(x-1)(x+1)/(x-1) = x+1
3Now substitute x = 1 into the simplified expression.1 + 1 = 2

blocks.x: Answer: lim_{x→1} (x²-1)/(x-1) = 2
Factoring a trinomial before cancelling
Evaluate lim_{x→4} (x²-7x+10)/(x²-4).

items: 1Direct substitution gives (16-28+10)/(16-4) = -2/12 — not indeterminate here, so this actually evaluates directly.-2/12 = -1/6

blocks.x: Rationalising the numerator
Evaluate lim_{x→9} (9-x)/(3-√x).

items: 1Direct substitution gives 0/0, so factor 9-x as a difference of squares in √x.9 - x = (3-√x)(3+√x)
2Cancel the common factor (3-√x).(3-√x)(3+√x)/(3-√x) = 3+√x
3Substitute x = 9 into the simplified expression.3 + √9 = 3 + 3 = 6

blocks.x: Answer: lim_{x→9} (9-x)/(3-√x) = 6
Left-hand and right-hand limits

lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) and lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) The left-hand limit lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) is the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the left. The right-hand limit lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) is the limit as x approaches a from the right. lim_{x→a} f(x) = L if and only if lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) = lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) = L. If the left- and right-hand limits disagree, the (two-sided) limit does not exist.
Determine the existence of lim_{x→2} f(x) when f(x) = 1-x for x ≤ 2, and f(x) = 4 for x > 2.

items: 1Approach from the left (x ≤ 2 branch applies): substitute x = 2 into 1-x.lim_{x→2⁻} f(x) = 1-2 = -1
2Approach from the right (x > 2 branch applies): the function is constant 4 near x=2 from the right.lim_{x→2⁺} f(x) = 4
3Compare the two one-sided limits.-1 ≠ 4

blocks.x: The left- and right-hand limits disagree, so lim_{x→2} f(x) does not exist.
Show that lim_{x→0} |x|/x does not exist.

items: 1For x > 0 (approaching from the right), |x| = x, so the expression simplifies.lim_{x→0⁺} x/x = lim_{x→0⁺} 1 = 1
2For x < 0 (approaching from the left), |x| = -x, so the expression simplifies differently.lim_{x→0⁻} (-x)/x = lim_{x→0⁻} -1 = -1
3The one-sided limits disagree: 1 ≠ -1.lim_{x→0⁺} ≠ lim_{x→0⁻}

blocks.x: lim_{x→0} |x|/x does not exist.

items: If the left-hand limit does not equal the right-hand limit, the limit does not exist.
The existence of lim_{x→a} f(x) does not depend on whether f(a) is defined.
The existence of lim_{x→a} f(x) does not depend on the value of f(a), if f(a) is defined.

blocks.x: Unbounded behaviour & trig limits
What happens to f(x) as x approaches 0 through very small values, or as x itself grows without bound — plus the special limit that underlies calculus of the trig functions.

lim_{x→0} 1/xⁿ As x gets closer to 0, xⁿ also gets closer to 0, and 1/xⁿ becomes very large. f(x) can be made arbitrarily large by taking x close enough to 0, so the limit does not exist in the ordinary sense — we write lim_{x→0} 1/xⁿ = ∞ to describe this behaviour. This is not treating ∞ as a number; it is notation for "increases without bound."
Describe the behaviour of f(x) = 1/x² as x → 0.

items: 1Compute f(x) for x-values shrinking toward 0: x = 0.1.f(0.1) = 1/0.01 = 100
3As x → 0, f(x) grows without bound in both directions (left and right), so no finite limit exists.f(x) → ∞

blocks.x: lim_{x→0} 1/x² = ∞ (limit does not exist as a finite number)
Limits as x → ∞

Three key facts (1) lim_{x→∞} 1/xⁿ = 0 if the index n is positive. (2) lim_{x→∞} xⁿ does not exist (grows without bound) if n is positive. (3) For a rational function lim_{x→∞} f(x)/g(x), first divide the numerator and denominator by the variable raised to the highest power of x that appears.
Evaluate lim_{x→∞} (5x²-1)/(2x²+1).

items: 1The highest power of x is x². Divide every term, top and bottom, by x².(5 - 1/x²) / (2 + 1/x²)
2As x → ∞, terms like 1/x² → 0 (Fact 1 above).→ (5 - 0)/(2 + 0)
3Simplify.= 5/2

blocks.x: Answer: lim_{x→∞} (5x²-1)/(2x²+1) = 5/2
Evaluate lim_{x→∞} 7x/(x-4).

items: 1Highest power of x is x¹. Divide numerator and denominator by x.7 / (1 - 4/x)

blocks.x: Answer: lim_{x→∞} 7x/(x-4) = 7
Evaluate lim_{x→∞} (2x³-7x+3)/(x³+2).

items: 1Highest power is x³. Divide every term by x³.(2 - 7/x² + 3/x³) / (1 + 2/x³)
2All the terms with x in the denominator vanish as x → ∞.→ (2 - 0 + 0)/(1 + 0)

blocks.x: Answer: lim_{x→∞} (2x³-7x+3)/(x³+2) = 2
Limit of simple trigonometric functions

lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1 Consider f(x) = sin x / x with x in radians. As x → 0, values of sin x/x get closer and closer to 1 from both sides, so lim_{x→0} sin x/x = 1. Related standard limits: lim cos x = 1, lim sin x = 0, lim tan x = 0 (all as x→0), and lim tan x/x = 1, lim sin 2x/2x... type expressions all reduce to the ratio pattern equalling 1.
Evaluate lim_{x→0} sin 2x / x.

items: 1Rewrite so the argument of sin matches the denominator, by multiplying and dividing by 2.sin 2x / x = 2 · sin 2x / 2x
2As x → 0, 2x → 0 too, so sin 2x / 2x → 1 by the standard limit.2 · lim_{2x→0} sin 2x / 2x = 2 · 1

blocks.x: Answer: lim_{x→0} sin 2x / x = 2
Show that lim_{x→0} tan x / x = 1.

items: 1Write tan x as sin x / cos x.tan x / x = (sin x / cos x) / x = (sin x / x) · (1 / cos x)
2Apply the product rule for limits (Theorem 6): the limit of a product is the product of the limits.lim (sin x/x) · lim (1/cos x)
3Evaluate each factor: sin x/x → 1, and 1/cos x → 1/cos 0 = 1/1 = 1.1 × 1 = 1

blocks.x: Answer: lim_{x→0} tan x/x = 1

blocks.x: No holes, gaps or jumps
A function is continuous if its graph can be drawn without lifting the pencil off the paper — this section turns that picture into a precise three-condition test.
Continuity, informally f is continuous if its graph has no breaks — no holes, gaps, or jumps. If the graph has a hole, a gap, or a jump at x = a, f is discontinuous at x = a.
The three-condition test
f is continuous at x = a if: (1) f(a) is defined. (2) lim_{x→a} f(x) exists. (3) f(a) = lim_{x→a} f(x). All three conditions must hold — if any one fails, f is discontinuous at a.
Continuity on an interval f(x) is continuous on an interval (a,b) if it is continuous for every value of x in that interval.
Testing continuity of a rational function
Verify the continuity of f(x) = (x²-4)/(x-2) at x = 2.

items: 1Condition 1: check whether f(2) is defined by substituting directly.f(2) = (4-4)/(2-2) = 0/0 — undefined!

blocks.x: f(2) is undefined, so Condition 1 fails — f is discontinuous at x = 2 (a removable "hole").
Testing continuity of a linear function
Determine the continuity of f(x) = 3x - 2 at x = -2.

items: 1Condition 1: is f(-2) defined? Yes — polynomials are defined everywhere.f(-2) = 3(-2) - 2 = -8
2Condition 2: does lim_{x→-2} f(x) exist? For a polynomial the limit always exists and equals direct substitution.lim_{x→-2} (3x-2) = -8
3Condition 3: does f(-2) equal the limit?-8 = -8 ✓

blocks.x: All three conditions hold — f is continuous at x = -2.
Testing continuity of a piecewise function
Test the continuity of f(x) = x+2 for x ≤ 1, and f(x) = x²+3 for x > 1, at x = 1.

items: 1Condition 1: f(1) uses the x ≤ 1 branch.f(1) = 1+2 = 3
2Condition 2: check the left-hand limit using the x ≤ 1 branch.lim_{x→1⁻} (x+2) = 1+2 = 3
3Check the right-hand limit using the x > 1 branch.lim_{x→1⁺} (x²+3) = 1+3 = 4
4Compare: the one-sided limits disagree (3 ≠ 4), so the two-sided limit does not exist.lim_{x→1⁻} ≠ lim_{x→1⁺}

blocks.x: Condition 2 fails (limit does not exist) — f is discontinuous at x = 1, with a jump.
Remarks — which functions are automatically continuous

c: For all real x except where the denominator is zero
For all real x in its domain
For all real x in its domain

blocks.x: Combining continuous functions If f and g are both continuous at a, and c is a constant, then the following are also continuous at a: f+g, f−g, cf, fg, and f/g (provided g(a) ≠ 0).
Interval of continuity
Determine the interval(s) within which f(x) = √(2x+3) is continuous.

items: 1A radical function is continuous on its domain, so find the domain: contents under the square root must be ≥ 0.2x + 3 ≥ 0
2Solve for x.2x ≥ -3 → x ≥ -3/2

blocks.x: f is continuous on [-3/2, ∞)
